questions.q: Per this lesson, why are experienced review panels, including CTA judges by multiple accounts, specifically trained to maintain a neutral expression?
options: So candidates can't use panelist facial reactions as a shortcut to figure out what answer is supposedly 'right'
Because panelists are not allowed to have personal opinions about a design
Because neutral expressions make panelists easier to photograph
Because showing any reaction is physically impossible to avoid
questions.explain: Trained neutrality is a deliberate design choice specifically meant to prevent candidates from reading approval or disapproval off panelist faces as a substitute for sound, self-contained reasoning.

questions.q: Which of these does this lesson identify as a signal still worth watching for, despite a panel's trained neutral expression?
options: Whether a panelist is smiling or frowning
A reviewer writing something down right after a specific statement, which often becomes a later question
The panel's overall mood at the start of the day
Whether the panelists are wearing formal or casual clothing
questions.explain: Note-taking right after a specific statement, follow-up questions clustering on the same topic, and whether reviewers visually follow a diagram as it's narrated are all harder-to-suppress signals worth watching -- facial expressions themselves are specifically trained to be unreliable.

questions.q: What does this lesson recommend doing if two consecutive panelist questions both circle back to the same part of your design?
options: Panic and completely improvise a new presentation from scratch
Treat it as useful information to weight remaining time and depth toward that area, without abandoning your overall prepared structure
Assume the panel is deliberately trying to confuse you and ignore the pattern
Immediately end the presentation since the design must be flawed
questions.explain: Reading the room productively means making small, deliberate adjustments -- weighting attention toward an area getting real scrutiny -- not scrapping the entire prepared approach over one pattern.

questions.q: What is the specific trap this lesson warns about regarding a panelist's blank or neutral expression?
options: Assuming a flat expression means the board is unimpressed, and reacting defensively (rushing, over-explaining) to a signal that -- given trained neutrality -- usually means nothing at all
Assuming a neutral expression always means the board is impressed
Believing that neutral expressions are only used by panels evaluating security architecture specifically
Thinking that neutral expressions are illegal under review board rules
questions.explain: Since boards are specifically trained toward neutrality, a flat expression usually signals nothing. Reacting to it as if it were negative feedback introduces a real problem (visible anxiety, lost structure) in response to an imagined one.

questions.q: Why does this lesson describe reading the room as a supporting skill rather than a substitute for substance?
options: Because reading the room is more important than the underlying design quality
Because it helps allocate attention well and avoid avoidable missteps, but cannot rescue a presentation where the design itself or its defense doesn't hold up
Because reading the room has no practical use at all in a review board
Because panels only evaluate body language and never evaluate the actual content
questions.explain: Reading the room is a refinement layered on top of substance -- useful for allocating attention and avoiding missteps, but it cannot compensate for a design or defense (covered in Lessons 4 and 5) that isn't actually sound.
